rationale: This socio-legal report clearly addresses water and sanitation access in informal Roma settlements in Sweden (C1), examines municipal administrative/legal enforcement mechanisms—specifically municipal evictions on sanitation grounds, informal settlement status of EU citizens, and municipal legal obligations regarding service provision (C2 narrow and plain)—and reports service exclusion/lack of alternative water and sanitation access beyond a few days (C4). While the reference to over 80 municipal evictions between 2013 and 2016 suggests plausible primary socio-legal empirical investigation (e.g., municipal data collection, case documentation, or fieldwork), the abstract does not explicitly state its empirical methods versus doctrinal human-rights analysis (C3 unclear), requiring full-text retrieval ('unsure').
plain_vs_narrow_note: No divergence between the narrow rule-type reading and literal/plain Criterion 2 wording: municipal eviction enforcement on sanitation grounds, informal settlement tenure/residency rules for vulnerable EU citizens, and municipal obligations to provide water and sanitation clearly satisfy both readings. Both decisions are 'unsure' solely because full-text inspection is needed to confirm Criterion 3 (whether the report presents primary socio-legal empirical data or purely doctrinal/normative legal analysis).

evidence_quotes.quote: Access to Water and Sanitation in Sweden's Informal Roma Settlements
Swedish municipalities initiated more than 80 evictions of vulnerable EU citizens, mostly Roma, from informal settlements on the grounds of poor sanitation between 2013 and 2016.
these evictions violated human rights obligations when individuals were offered no alternative access to water and sanitation beyond a few days.
